title: Chills After Drinking: Why Alcohol Makes You Cold and Shivery
excerpt: Why you get chills, cold sweats, or shivers after drinking alcohol, how to warm up safely, and the warning signs of hypothermia, alcohol poisoning, or withdrawal.
metaDescription: Why alcohol gives you chills and cold sweats: heat loss, low blood sugar, and poor sleep. How to warm up, and when chills after drinking need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** chills after drinking are common, and in most social drinkers they come from a few ordinary effects of alcohol on the body. Alcohol widens the blood vessels in your skin, so you feel warm while you're actually losing heat. It blunts the part of your brain that keeps your temperature steady. It can push your blood sugar down, especially if you drank without eating. And it wrecks your sleep, which leaves you shivery and run-down the next morning. Those causes usually fade within a day once you've eaten, had some fluids, and warmed up.

There are a few situations where chills are not a normal hangover: being very cold or hard to wake after heavy drinking (a sign of alcohol poisoning or hypothermia), a real fever measured with a thermometer, and chills with shaking and sweating a day or two after someone who drinks heavily every day stops. Those need medical attention, and the box below says exactly when.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if someone who has been drinking is cold to the touch, pale or bluish, very confused, hard to wake or can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or keeps vomiting while drowsy. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and low body temperature is one of them. Don't leave the person to "sleep it off"; keep them on their side and stay with them until help arrives. **Get medical care promptly if** your temperature is 100.4°F (38°C) or higher and doesn't settle, chills come with a stiff neck, a new rash, trouble breathing, chest pain, or severe belly pain, you have diabetes and feel shaky, sweaty, or confused after drinking, or chills last more than a day or two. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, chills, a racing heart, or feel very anxious within a day or two of cutting back, that can be alcohol withdrawal. It can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than trying to tough it out.

## Why Do I Get Chills After Drinking Alcohol?

Your body works hard to keep its core temperature in a narrow range. A region of the brain called the hypothalamus acts as the thermostat. When you get cold, it tells the blood vessels in your skin to narrow so less heat escapes, and if that isn't enough, it makes your muscles shiver to produce heat. When you get hot, it does the reverse: it opens up the skin's blood vessels and turns on sweating.

Alcohol interferes with almost every step of that system. The chills you feel are the result of several things happening at once, and which one dominates depends on how much you drank, whether you ate, the temperature around you, and how well you slept. Here are the main causes, roughly in order of how often they're to blame.

### 1. Alcohol makes you lose heat while feeling warm

This is the big one, and it's also why the "warm glow" of a drink is misleading. Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes and widens blood vessels, especially the small ones near the surface of the skin. Warm blood moves from your core toward your skin. You feel that as a pleasant flush of warmth, and your cheeks may go pink.

But your skin is where heat leaves the body. With more warm blood sitting near the surface, you shed heat into the air faster than usual. Your core temperature drifts down even while your skin feels toasty. When the alcohol starts to wear off, or when you step outside, or when you finally lie still in bed, you notice how cold you've actually become, and the shivers start.

This effect is well documented, and it's why public-health and outdoor-safety guidance consistently warns against drinking alcohol to "warm up." The idea of a nip of brandy for someone stuck in the snow is a myth that does real harm.

### 2. Alcohol weakens your shivering and temperature control

On top of the heat loss, alcohol dulls the hypothalamus itself and the reflexes it controls. The normal response to cold (narrowing the skin's blood vessels and starting to shiver) kicks in later and less strongly after a few drinks. Alcohol also blunts your sense of being cold, so you're slower to put on a jacket, close a window, or get under the covers.

At ordinary social-drinking levels this mostly means you cool down a bit more than you otherwise would. At heavy levels it becomes dangerous, which is why low body temperature is one of the recognized signs of alcohol poisoning and why intoxication is a well-known risk factor for hypothermia in cold weather.

### 3. Low blood sugar

Your liver has two jobs that matter here. It breaks down alcohol, and it keeps your blood sugar steady between meals by releasing stored sugar and making new sugar. When the liver is busy processing alcohol, it gets worse at making new glucose. If you drank on an empty stomach, skipped dinner, danced for hours, or slept through breakfast, your blood sugar can dip.

Low blood sugar causes a familiar cluster of symptoms: shakiness, sweating, feeling cold and clammy, a fast heartbeat, irritability, hunger, and trouble thinking clearly. Many people describe "the chills" when what they're actually feeling is a mild blood-sugar drop. This is one reason chills so often show up in the early morning, hours after the last drink and long after the last meal.

For most healthy people the dip is mild and a meal fixes it. It's a much bigger concern for people with diabetes, especially those using insulin or certain tablets that lower blood sugar, because alcohol can make a low much deeper and harder to notice. Our [guide to alcohol and blood sugar](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) covers that in detail.

### 4. Fluid loss

Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink by suppressing vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Add sweating on a dance floor or in a hot bar, and maybe some vomiting, and you can wake up short on fluids. Being dehydrated doesn't directly make you cold, but it leaves you feeling weak, lightheaded, and achy, and it makes everything else feel worse. It also tends to travel with poor sleep and low blood sugar. (For how much alcohol actually dries you out, see [does alcohol dehydrate you?](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you))

### 5. Broken sleep and the rebound effect

Alcohol helps you fall asleep but disrupts the second half of the night. As your body finishes clearing the alcohol, there's a rebound: your nervous system becomes more alert than usual. That can mean waking at 3 or 4 a.m., a racing heart, sweating, and then feeling chilled as the sweat cools on your skin. If you've ever kicked off the covers drenched and then lain there shivering, this is the cycle. Our guides to [night sweats after drinking](/never-hungover/night-sweats-after-drinking) and [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) go deeper on this.

Poor sleep on its own also makes people feel colder. After a short, fragmented night, many of us feel chilly and run-down the next day regardless of what we drank.

### 6. The hangover's inflammatory "flu-ish" feeling

Researchers who study hangovers have found that the morning after heavy drinking involves a low-grade inflammatory response, with changes in the immune system's signaling molecules. That's part of why a bad hangover feels so much like coming down with something: aches, tiredness, feeling hot and cold, and wanting to stay in bed. It usually doesn't produce a true fever, but it can produce chills and that shivery, out-of-sorts feeling. If you're not sure whether you have a hangover or an actual illness, our guide to [hangover fever](/never-hungover/hangover-fever) walks through how to tell.

## Chills While Drinking vs. Chills the Next Day

The timing is a useful clue to the cause.

**Chills while you're still drinking or soon after.** This is usually heat loss. You've been sitting near the door, standing outside on a patio, walking home in the cold, or the venue's air conditioning is blasting, and your widened skin blood vessels are letting heat pour out. Getting somewhere warm and putting on a layer usually fixes it quickly. If someone is very drunk *and* cold, take that more seriously (see the hypothermia section below).

**Chills in the middle of the night.** This tends to be the rebound and sweating cycle, sometimes combined with low blood sugar. Waking soaked, then cold, with a pounding heart is classic.

**Chills the next morning or afternoon.** This is usually a mix of low blood sugar, fluid loss, bad sleep, and the general inflammatory hangover. A meal, fluids, and warmth tend to help within a few hours.

**Chills starting a day or more after drinking, getting worse rather than better.** That pattern doesn't fit a normal hangover. Think about an infection, food poisoning, or (in someone who drinks heavily every day and has stopped) alcohol withdrawal.

## Why Do I Feel Cold After Drinking When I Felt Warm Before?

This is one of the most common questions, and it comes straight from the first two causes above. The warm feeling from a drink is your skin heating up because blood has moved there. Your core, the part that matters for staying healthy, is actually losing heat. Once the alcohol wears off and your blood vessels tighten back up, the warm skin sensation disappears, and you're left with a slightly cooler body that you now notice. Lying still in bed, when you're no longer moving around to make heat, often makes it more obvious.

So feeling warm and then cold isn't two separate problems. It's the same effect, felt from two sides.

## Cold Sweats After Drinking

Cold sweats, where your skin is damp and clammy but you feel chilled, are worth separating from ordinary night sweats.

The usual harmless explanations are the rebound effect during sleep and a mild blood-sugar dip. Both trigger your stress response, which releases adrenaline. Adrenaline makes you sweat and narrows the blood vessels in your skin at the same time, so you end up damp *and* cold. A fast heartbeat often comes along with it (see [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking)).

Cold sweats deserve more attention when they come with chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, fainting, severe belly pain, confusion, or a feeling that something is badly wrong. Those can point to a heart problem or another emergency that has nothing to do with the hangover, so call 911 rather than assuming it's the alcohol.

## Shivering and Shaking After Drinking: Chills or Tremor?

People use "the shakes" for two different things, and it helps to tell them apart.

**Shivering** is your muscles rapidly tightening and relaxing to make heat. It comes in waves, it usually comes with feeling cold and maybe goosebumps, and it eases when you warm up.

**Tremor** is a fine trembling, often most noticeable in your hands when you hold them out or try to do something precise like texting or holding a cup. After a night of drinking, a mild tremor is common and usually comes from low blood sugar, poor sleep, and the nervous system's rebound as alcohol leaves the body. It typically fades over the day. Our [hangover shakes guide](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) covers this in more depth.

The two often happen together, which is why "I woke up with chills and shakes" is such a common description of a rough morning.

What matters is the context. For an occasional social drinker after a big night, both are almost always temporary. For someone who drinks heavily every day, tremor, sweating, and chills that start within a day or two of stopping can be the early stage of alcohol withdrawal. Withdrawal can progress to seizures or a dangerous state called delirium tremens, so it needs medical advice, not willpower. A doctor can make stopping much safer.

## Can Drinking Alcohol Cause Hypothermia?

Yes. Alcohol is one of the best-known contributors to hypothermia, which is when your core body temperature falls below about 95°F (35°C). It does this in three ways at once: it makes you lose heat through your skin, it weakens your shivering response, and it dulls your judgment and your sense of being cold, so you don't take obvious steps to protect yourself.

Social drinkers mostly encounter this in a few specific situations:

- Walking home in winter, especially if you get lost, sit down to rest, or fall asleep outside
- Passing out somewhere cold, like a porch, a car, or a cold room
- Swimming or being in cold water after drinking, since water pulls heat from the body much faster than air
- Outdoor events, camping, skiing, or tailgating in cold or wet weather

Early hypothermia looks like shivering, clumsy hands, slurred speech, and confusion. That's a problem when the person is drunk, because those are exactly the signs you'd expect from alcohol, so friends often miss it. As it gets worse, the shivering can actually *stop*, which is a bad sign rather than a good one, and the person becomes very drowsy and hard to rouse.

If you find someone who has been drinking and is cold, confused, or hard to wake, call 911. While you wait, get them somewhere warm, remove wet clothing, cover them with blankets (including the head and neck), and keep them on their side in case they vomit. Don't put them in a hot bath, and don't give them more alcohol.

## Is It Alcohol Poisoning?

Low body temperature is on the list of alcohol poisoning signs from the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, alongside confusion, vomiting, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, pale or bluish skin, and being hard to wake or unresponsive. A person doesn't need to have all of these for it to be an emergency.

The key difference from an ordinary rough night is how the person responds. Someone with a hangover is miserable but awake and making sense. Someone with alcohol poisoning may be cold and clammy *and* confused, drowsy, or impossible to rouse. Blood alcohol can keep rising after someone stops drinking, because alcohol already in the stomach is still being absorbed, so don't wait to see whether they improve. Call 911.

## Could It Be Something Other Than the Alcohol?

Chills are a symptom with a lot of possible causes, and the night you went drinking might simply be the night you also caught something. Think about these:

**A viral infection.** Flu, COVID, and other viruses often start with chills, body aches, and tiredness, which feel very similar to a hangover. Crowded bars and parties are good places to pick them up. A measured fever, a sore throat, a cough, or symptoms that get worse on day two point toward an infection rather than the drink. (See [hangover fever](/never-hungover/hangover-fever) for a side-by-side comparison.)

**Food poisoning.** Late-night food, buffet dishes, and street food after drinking are common culprits. Chills with vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach cramps that start several hours after eating suggest food poisoning.

**Alcohol intolerance or a histamine reaction.** Some people flush, get a stuffy nose, feel hot and then cold, or get hives after even small amounts of alcohol, particularly wine and beer. That's a different issue from a hangover. Our guide to [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) explains the causes and what helps.

**Medications.** Some medicines interact with alcohol and can cause flushing, sweating, chills, nausea, or a pounding heart. Examples include metronidazole and some other antibiotics, certain diabetes medicines, and disulfiram. If you take a regular medication and get chills, sweating, or flushing after drinking, ask your pharmacist whether the two interact.

**Low thyroid, anemia, or simply being run down.** If you feel cold all the time, not just after drinking, alcohol may be making an existing problem more noticeable. That's worth mentioning to a doctor.

**Pancreatitis.** It's uncommon, but heavy drinking can inflame the pancreas. Severe upper belly pain that may spread to the back, with vomiting, fever, or chills, needs urgent care.

## How to Stop Chills After Drinking

For a normal hangover-type chill, the fixes are simple and they mostly target the causes above.

**Warm up gradually.** Put on layers, socks, and a hat, get under a blanket, and drink something warm like herbal tea or broth. A warm (not hot) shower can feel good once you're steady on your feet. Avoid scalding baths if you're still intoxicated or lightheaded, since alcohol already lowers blood pressure and fainting in a bathroom is a real injury risk.

**Eat something with carbohydrates.** If low blood sugar is part of the problem, food is the fastest fix. Toast, crackers, a banana, oatmeal, or juice followed by a proper meal can quickly ease the shaky, cold, clammy feeling. Eggs and other protein help keep you steady afterward.

**Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water through the morning rather than chugging a liter at once, especially if your stomach is upset. An electrolyte drink can help if you've been sweating, vomiting, or have diarrhea.

**Rest, but stay in a warm room.** Sleep makes up for some of the broken night. Just make sure the room isn't cold and you're not lying in damp sheets or clothes after sweating.

**Don't drink more alcohol.** The "hair of the dog" just restarts the heat loss and pushes the problem a few hours down the road.

**Be careful with painkillers.** If you're achy, remember that acetaminophen (Tylenol) and alcohol both put work on the liver, and ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated. If you use either, take a single standard dose with food once the alcohol has cleared, and don't take acetaminophen if you drink heavily on a regular basis without asking a doctor first. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the details. Painkillers lower a fever, so check your temperature *before* taking one if you're unsure whether you're sick.

**Take your temperature.** It takes a minute and answers the most important question. Feeling cold with a normal reading is a hangover. A reading of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher means something else may be going on.

## How Long Do Chills After Drinking Last?

For most people, hangover chills ease within a few hours of eating, rehydrating, and warming up, and they're gone within a day. Alcohol-related symptoms in general peak around the time blood alcohol returns to zero and then improve over the following hours. (See [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) for more on the timeline.)

Chills that last more than a day or two, keep coming back without drinking, get worse instead of better, or come with a measured fever are not typical of a hangover and are worth getting checked.

## How to Prevent Chills After Drinking

The best prevention lines up with the causes.

- **Eat before and while you drink.** A meal with some carbohydrates, protein, and fat slows alcohol absorption and makes a blood-sugar dip less likely. A snack before bed helps too.
- **Pace yourself.** Fewer drinks, spread out, means less heat loss, less rebound, and a smaller hit to sleep. Alternating each drink with water is a simple way to do this.
- **Dress for the trip home, not the bar.** The bar may be warm, but the walk or wait for a ride often isn't. Bring the jacket.
- **Plan a safe way home.** Never walk home alone drunk in the cold, and look out for friends who wander off or doze somewhere outside.
- **Keep your bedroom comfortable.** Have a blanket handy, keep a glass of water by the bed, and consider a spare T-shirt in case you wake up sweaty.
- **Don't drink when you're already getting sick.** If you're starting to feel run-down, alcohol makes it harder to tell what's going on and harder for your body to cope.

For more on what reliably makes the morning after easier, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Does DHM Help With Chills After Drinking?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's sold as a hangover supplement. Most of the research on it is in animals and cell studies, with only limited human data. That research suggests it may support the liver's processing of alcohol and counter some of alcohol's effects on brain receptors.

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents chills, protects you from hypothermia, or treats any of the more serious causes covered above. It doesn't change the basic advice: eat, pace yourself, dress warmly, and get help for the warning signs. If you'd like to try it as part of a sensible drinking routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get chills after drinking alcohol?**

Mostly because alcohol widens the blood vessels in your skin, so you lose body heat while feeling warm, and it weakens your brain's temperature control and shivering response. Low blood sugar, fluid loss, and broken sleep add to it the next morning. For most social drinkers it passes within a day after food, fluids, and warmth.

**Why do I feel cold after drinking when I felt warm before?**

The warm feeling is blood moving to your skin, where it gives off heat. Your core is actually cooling down. When the alcohol wears off and your skin blood vessels tighten again, the warm sensation fades and you notice that your body has lost heat, especially once you're lying still.

**Are chills the next day a sign of a hangover or the flu?**

Chills are common in both. A hangover usually improves over the day once you eat and drink fluids, and it rarely causes a measured fever. A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, a sore throat, a cough, or symptoms that get worse on day two point toward an infection. Take your temperature before using any fever-reducing painkiller.

**Can drinking alcohol cause hypothermia?**

Yes. Alcohol increases heat loss through the skin, weakens shivering, and dulls your sense of being cold. It's a well-known risk factor for hypothermia, especially for people walking home in cold weather, falling asleep outside, or going into cold water. If someone who has been drinking is cold, confused, or hard to wake, call 911.

**Why do I get cold sweats after drinking?**

Usually from the rebound effect as alcohol leaves your system during sleep, or from a mild drop in blood sugar. Both trigger adrenaline, which makes you sweat while narrowing your skin's blood vessels, so you feel damp and cold at the same time. Cold sweats with chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or confusion need emergency care.

**Can chills after drinking be alcohol withdrawal?**

In someone who drinks heavily most days, chills, sweating, shaking, a racing heart, and anxiety that start within a day or two of cutting back can be withdrawal. It can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than stopping suddenly on your own. In an occasional social drinker, chills after a big night are much more likely to be an ordinary hangover.

**Does a warm shower help chills after drinking?**

A warm, not hot, shower can help once you're sober and steady on your feet. Avoid very hot baths or showers while still intoxicated or lightheaded, because alcohol lowers blood pressure and fainting is a real risk. Layers, a blanket, a warm drink, and some food are usually enough.

**How long do chills after drinking last?**

Typical hangover chills ease within a few hours of eating and warming up and are usually gone within a day. Chills lasting more than a day or two, getting worse, or coming with a measured fever aren't typical of a hangover and are worth getting checked.
